# Use Claude to Read and Explain a Long Contract or Legal Document

> **In short:** You can paste a rental agreement, terms of service, or employment contract into Claude and ask it to summarize the key points in plain English. It's fast, free to try, and works best when you frame the request as a specific question — Claude can't replace a lawyer, but it can save you an hour of squinting.

Got a 30-page PDF that nobody on Earth would actually read end-to-end? You can hand the text to Claude and ask, in your own words, "what does this actually say?" This guide walks through the whole flow: getting the contract onto your screen, dropping it into Claude, and asking the right questions. No legal background needed.

## Before you start
- **A Claude account**, free or paid — sign up at `claude.ai` (the free plan covers most personal use; the paid tier gives you a larger context window, which matters for very long contracts).
- **The contract itself** — a PDF, an email attachment, or a webpage you're copying from. Aim for a digital copy, not a photo of paper, because text copies are far more accurate.
- **A way to extract the text** if it's a PDF — most computers let you select-and-copy from a PDF, or you can use a free online tool. macOS and Windows both have built-in PDF text selection.
- **Rough total time**: 10–15 minutes the first time, around 5 minutes once you've done it once.

> ⚠️ **What Claude can't do.** Claude is an AI assistant, not a lawyer. It can summarize and explain, but it cannot give you legal advice, predict how a court would rule, or know which laws apply in your specific situation. For anything with real consequences — signing a lease, accepting a job offer, disputing a charge — run the summary past a human professional.

## Step 1 — Get the text out of the document
Open the contract as a PDF or webpage and **copy the text** the way you would from any other file: click at the start, hold **Shift** and click at the end, then press **Ctrl+C** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd+C** (macOS). On a phone, long-press in the text and choose **Select All**, then **Copy**.
You'll know it worked when your clipboard now holds a wall of highlighted-looking text you can paste anywhere (for example, into a notes app to test).
**If it looks different:** some PDFs lock their text behind scanned images. If your **Select All** only grabs a few words or you see nothing highlighted at all, open the PDF in a viewer like Adobe Acrobat Reader, Google Drive, or your browser — they sometimes unlock the text layer. If that fails, use a free "PDF to text" tool online, or simply type the headings you can see into Claude and ask it to explain what those usually mean. Don't paste a screenshot: Claude works with text.

## Step 2 — Open Claude and start a fresh chat
Go to `claude.ai` in your browser, sign in, and click **New chat** in the sidebar (top-left). A blank conversation box appears at the bottom of the screen — that's where your message and document will both go.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with a **Send** arrow (▶) and a paperclip-shaped attach icon nearby.
**If it looks different:** some accounts land directly in a recent conversation. Just look for a **+ New chat** or **Start new conversation** button at the top of the left sidebar. On the mobile app the same **+** or pencil icon in the corner does the same thing.

## Step 3 — Paste the contract and ask your first question
Click inside the message box and press **Ctrl+V** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd+V** (macOS) to paste the long block of contract text *into the same message* as your question. Then add a clear request on a new line, like the example below, and hit **Send**.
💬 Example: "Here's the rental agreement I was sent. In plain language, what am I actually agreeing to? Highlight anything unusual or that renters often overlook."
You'll know it worked when Claude replies with a structured summary — usually with headings like *Key terms*, *Your obligations*, *What to watch out for* — instead of just repeating the text back at you.
**If it looks different:** if Claude's reply is short or seems generic, it may have ignored your question. Just send a second message asking for a clearer summary. Also: if the contract is *very* long, you might hit a "this is too long in one go" notice — move to **Step 4** for that workaround.

## Step 4 — Break the document into chunks if you got the "too long" notice
Claude can read a lot at once, but huge contracts can overflow that limit. **Open a notes app** and split the contract text into rough sections by hand: "Section 1 — Parties," "Section 2 — Term and Rent," "Section 3 — Deposits," and so on. Then send each chunk in its own message, with one short question per chunk.
💬 Example: "[Paste section 1 here] In one paragraph, summarize what this section says and flag anything I should negotiate."
You'll know it worked when each section gets its own focused answer and a small "what to watch out for" line. At the end, ask: "Based on everything I've pasted, give me a 5-bullet summary of the whole contract and the three most important things to push back on."
**If it looks different:** if you don't want to split the file manually, paid Claude plans have a much bigger context window (think of this as Claude's short-term memory: how much text it can keep in mind during one chat) and often fit a long contract without splitting. The "Artifacts" feature on the same paid tier can also let Claude read a directly uploaded PDF in one go — look for a small paperclip or upload button near the message box.

## Step 5 — Ask targeted follow-up questions
Now that Claude has the document in its context (the chat's working memory: everything you've sent and received so far in this conversation), you can ask it pointed questions without re-pasting anything. This is where the real time-saving happens — most contracts only have four or five questions that actually matter to you.
💬 Example: "Can I get my security deposit back if I move out 30 days early?" or "If they change the price mid-contract, am I locked in?" or "What's the worst part of this agreement for me as the renter?"
You'll know it worked when Claude pulls a specific clause out of the text — usually with the section or clause number — and translates it into everyday language.
**If it looks different:** if Claude's answer feels vague, ask it to "quote the actual sentence from the contract" first, then re-explain it. That trick forces it to ground its answer in the real text instead of guessing.

## Step 6 — Save the summary somewhere you'll find it
Once you have a summary you trust, click the small **copy** icon at the corner of Claude's reply, or highlight the text and copy it the usual way. Paste it into an email to yourself, a note in your phone, or a shared doc with anyone who also needs to know.
💬 Example: "Save these notes and remind me to ask the landlord about the early-termination fee before I sign."
You'll know it worked when you have a plain-English record of the contract's main points, separate from the original legal document, that you can re-read in under five minutes.
**If it looks different:** Claude's chat history stays in your sidebar by default and you can reopen it from any device you're signed into. If you want a downloadable file, ask Claude: "Turn this summary into a Markdown checklist I can save" — it'll output one in chat that you can copy into a `.md` file.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting a photo or screenshot of the contract.** Claude reads text, not images — unless you're using a feature that explicitly accepts images. Type or copy the actual text first.
- **Asking one giant question like "explain this contract."** You'll get a wishy-washy answer. Ask for specific things: the cancellation terms, the fees, who's responsible for repairs, the auto-renewal clause.
- **Trusting the summary without checking.** Claude sometimes misreads a number or a date. If something matters to you, ask Claude to quote the original sentence so you can compare. For anything serious — money, a job, a home — confirm with a real lawyer or a free legal-aid clinic.
- **Sharing private contracts in public chats or forums.** Treat contract text like you would any sensitive document: only paste it into a private Claude chat tied to your own account.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Before you click "I agree" on a new app's terms of service, the cleaning service's policy, or your kid's summer-camp registration, drop the text into Claude and ask "what's the catch?" You'll catch auto-renewal clauses and data-sharing sections that most people miss.
- **For your business or work:** When a client or vendor emails a 20-page service agreement, you can have a plain-English brief waiting in your inbox within minutes instead of bookmarking it for "later." Bring the brief — and your annotated questions — to whoever signs things for your business.
- **If you're just getting started:** Your very first move should be the one below. Don't wait for a "big" contract to try this. A short terms-of-service page works fine to learn how to ask the right questions.

## Try it now
Pick one document in your email right now — even a four-paragraph cancellation policy from a gym or a streaming service you forgot to cancel. Paste it into a new Claude chat and ask: *"In plain language, what does this actually let them do? What's the catch?"* You'll have your answer in under a minute, and you'll know exactly how to repeat this the next time something bigger shows up.
